dossier_sections.heading: Why we own it
dossier_sections.text: Why we own Nu is the largest digital bank in Latin America, operating under the Nubank brand across Brazil, Mexico and Colombia. They have 139mn customers with 118mn in Brazil, where it now touches well over half the adult population, 16mn in Mexico, where management says it has become the country's largest digital bank, and 5+mn in Colombia, its earliest-stage market. The product set spans the full retail-banking stack, from deposit accounts, credit cards, personal and secured lending to insurance, investing, and, more recently, Nu Global, a multicurrency account live in 35+ countries offering yield, fee-free FX transfers and crypto trading. Nu's business model is a licensed, deposit-funded bank that gathers low-cost deposits (cost of deposits running at 88% of interbank rates), extends credit against them, and gets paid through net interest margin, interchange and fees. The moat is a cost-to-serve structure that legacy banks in the region cannot replicate without cannibalizing their own branch networks. Nu's cost to serve per active customer in Brazil (currently $1/month) runs 85% lower than incumbents. That structural gap sits on top of a physical-footprint difference. Nu runs on zero branches and 8,000 employees in Brazil versus Itaú's 16,000+ branches/ATMs and Bradesco's 82,000+ headcount. Nu's NuFormer AI foundation model now powers credit decisioning, customer service and growth targeting across the full customer base, and management notes that customers where Nu is the primary banking relationship show delinquency of half the portfolio average. The data advantage compounds through underwriting, with the flywheel functioning as a genuine risk- management edge, not just a marketing one. Nu sizes the serviceable addressable market, or the revenue potential of retail financial services in Brazil, Mexico and Colombia, measured as interest income plus service fees minus funding costs, at $213bn+ in 2024. Capital allocation is a real point of differentiation versus both fintech peers still burning cash to grow and incumbent banks funding growth with dilutive capital raises. This is self-funded compounding, which is a materially cleaner capital story than most high-growth financials. With Brazil still under-monetized relative to its penetration, Mexico repeating the early Brazil trajectory against a well- documented unbanked base (World Bank's 2025 Global Findex report names Mexico as one of just eight countries holding over half the world's roughly 1.3bn unbanked adults), Colombia providing a third, earlier-stage leg, and an AI-driven underwriting edge that's showing up in the delinquency data rather than just the marketing deck, Nu should remain a core position in PFOE.

basis.claim: The subject shows strong documented fundamentals, with revenue up 37.0% to US$15,774.8 million and net income up 45.6% to US$2,871.7 million in 2025.

Identified subject risks are real but disclosed: gross margin fell to 42.0% from 45.6%, frontloaded ECL depresses gross profit while adding customers, and regulatory ring-fencing limits intra-group asset transfers.
